claims.text: An ultrathin graded WC interlayer can be incorporated at the W–Cu interface by co-deposition or controlled-reaction processing.
The WC interlayer forms a graded transition layer between the W and Cu phases.
The graded WC interlayer reduces interfacial defects.
The graded WC interlayer reduces stress concentrations at the W–Cu interface.
The WC interlayer minimizes phonon scattering at the W–Cu interface.
Reduced phonon scattering lowers thermal boundary resistance.
The WC interlayer is robust under irradiation and high-temperature exposure.
The irradiation and high-temperature robustness of the WC interlayer helps preserve the mechanical integrity of the composite.
A gradual transition in bonding and lattice parameters reduces interfacial strain.
A gradual transition in bonding and lattice parameters reduces potential sites for radiation damage.
The WC-interlayered W–Cu composite will have approximately 10% or greater thermal-conductivity improvement relative to an otherwise comparable composite without the interlayer.
The WC-interlayered composite will retain mechanical durability comparable to that of the control composite.
The WC-interlayered composite will retain irradiation resistance comparable to that of the control composite.
Conventional W–Cu composites without the WC interlayer have higher interfacial thermal resistance.
The beneficial effect requires an optimized WC interlayer thickness, likely in the nanometer range, and a well-controlled WC phase.
An excessively thick or discontinuous WC layer may degrade mechanical integrity or create additional thermal barriers.
The predicted benefits should persist under high temperatures, cyclic thermal loading, and irradiation exposure relevant to heat-dissipation and fusion-reactor applications.
